doc:
Given a bijection from a finite set `s` to a finite set `t`, the cardinalities of `s` and `t`
are equal.

The difference with `Finset.card_bij'` is that the bijection is specified as a surjective injection,
rather than by an inverse function.

The difference with `Finset.card_nbij` is that the bijection is allowed to use membership of the
domain, rather than being a non-dependent function.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} {s : Finset α} {t : Finset β} (i : (a : α) → a ∈ s → β),
  (∀ (a : α) (ha : a ∈ s), i a ha ∈ t) →
    (∀ (a₁ : α) (ha₁ : a₁ ∈ s) (a₂ : α) (ha₂ : a₂ ∈ s), i a₁ ha₁ = i a₂ ha₂ → a₁ = a₂) →
      (∀ b ∈ t, ∃ a, ∃ (ha : a ∈ s), i a ha = b) → s.card = t.card

doc:
Given a bijection from a finite set `s` to a finite set `t`, the cardinalities of `s` and `t`
are equal.

The difference with `Finset.card_bij` is that the bijection is specified with an inverse, rather
than as a surjective injection.

The difference with `Finset.card_nbij'` is that the bijection and its inverse are allowed to use
membership of the domains, rather than being non-dependent functions.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} {s : Finset α} {t : Finset β} (i : (a : α) → a ∈ s → β) (j : (a : β) → a ∈ t → α)
  (hi : ∀ (a : α) (ha : a ∈ s), i a ha ∈ t) (hj : ∀ (a : β) (ha : a ∈ t), j a ha ∈ s),
  (∀ (a : α) (ha : a ∈ s), j (i a ha) ⋯ = a) → (∀ (a : β) (ha : a ∈ t), i (j a ha) ⋯ = a) → s.card = t.card

doc:
Given a bijection from a finite set `s` to a finite set `t`, the cardinalities of `s` and `t`
are equal.

The difference with `Finset.card_nbij'` is that the bijection is specified as a surjective
injection, rather than by an inverse function.

The difference with `Finset.card_bij` is that the bijection is a non-dependent function, rather than
being allowed to use membership of the domain.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} {s : Finset α} {t : Finset β} (i : α → β),
  Set.MapsTo i ↑s ↑t → Set.InjOn i ↑s → Set.SurjOn i ↑s ↑t → s.card = t.card

doc:
Given a bijection from a finite set `s` to a finite set `t`, the cardinalities of `s` and `t`
are equal.

The difference with `Finset.card_nbij` is that the bijection is specified with an inverse, rather
than as a surjective injection.

The difference with `Finset.card_bij'` is that the bijection and its inverse are non-dependent
functions, rather than being allowed to use membership of the domains.

The difference with `Finset.card_equiv` is that bijectivity is only required to hold on the domains,
rather than on the entire types.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} {s : Finset α} {t : Finset β} (i : α → β) (j : β → α),
  Set.MapsTo i ↑s ↑t → Set.MapsTo j ↑t ↑s → Set.LeftInvOn j i ↑s → Set.RightInvOn j i ↑t → s.card = t.card

∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} (p : α → Prop) [inst : DecidablePred p] [inst_1 : (x : α) → Decidable ¬p x],
  (Finset.filter p s).card + {a ∈ s | ¬p a}.card = s.card

doc:
Given a subset `s` of a set `t`, of sizes at most and at least `n` respectively, there exists a
set `u` of size `n` which is both a superset of `s` and a subset of `t`.
statement: ∀ {α : Type u_1} {s t : Finset α} {n : ℕ}, s ⊆ t → s.card ≤ n → n ≤ t.card → ∃ u, s ⊆ u ∧ u ⊆ t ∧ u.card = n

doc: We can shrink a set to any smaller size.
statement: ∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {n : ℕ}, n ≤ s.card → ∃ t ⊆ s, t.card = n
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {n : ℕ}, n ≤ s.card ↔ ∃ t ⊆ s, t.card = n

∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq α] {X Y : Finset α} {n : ℕ},
  2 * n < (X ∪ Y).card → ∃ C, n < C.card ∧ (C ⊆ X ∨ C ⊆ Y)
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.card = 1 ↔ ∃ a, s = {a}
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.card = 1 ↔ ∃! a, a ∈ s
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s t : Finset α} [inst : DecidableEq α], (∃ a ∉ s, insert a s = t) ↔ s ⊆ t ∧ s.card + 1 = t.card
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.card ≤ 1 ↔ ∀ a ∈ s, ∀ b ∈ s, a = b
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.card ≤ 1 ↔ ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ s → b ∈ s → a = b
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.card ≤ 1 ↔ Subsingleton ↥s

doc: A finset has cardinality at most 1 iff its underlying set is subsingleton.
statement: ∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.card ≤ 1 ↔ (↑s).Subsingleton
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} [Nonempty α], s.card ≤ 1 ↔ ∃ x, s ⊆ {x}
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, 1 < s.card → ∀ (a : α), ∃ b ∈ s, b ≠ a

doc: A `Finset` of a subsingleton type has cardinality at most one.
statement: ∀ {α : Type u_1} [Subsingleton α] (s : Finset α), s.card ≤ 1
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, 1 < s.card ↔ ∃ a ∈ s, ∃ b ∈ s, a ≠ b
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, 1 < s.card ↔ ∃ a b, a ∈ s ∧ b ∈ s ∧ a ≠ b
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, 1 < s.card ↔ s.Nontrivial
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.Nontrivial → 1 < s.card
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, s.Nontrivial → 2 ≤ s.card

doc:
Given an injective map `f : α → β` for finite sets `s ⊂ α` and `t ⊂ β` such that `t` has
cardinality one more than `s`, there exists a unique element of `t` not in `f(s)`.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} {s : Finset α} {f : α → β} {t : Finset β} [inst : DecidableEq β],
  Set.InjOn f ↑s → Set.MapsTo f ↑s ↑t → t.card = s.card + 1 → ∃! x, x ∈ t ∧ x ∉ Finset.image f s

doc:
If a Finset in a Pi type is nontrivial (has at least two elements), then
its projection to some factor is nontrivial, and the fibers of the projection
are proper subsets.
statement:
∀ {ι : Type u_3} {α : ι → Type u_4} [inst : (i : ι) → DecidableEq (α i)] {s : Finset ((i : ι) → α i)},
  1 < s.card → ∃ i, 1 < (Finset.image (fun x => x i) s).card ∧ ∀ (ai : α i), {x ∈ s | x i = ai} ⊂ s
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {n : ℕ}, s.card = n + 1 ↔ ∃ a t, ∃ (h : a ∉ t), Finset.cons a t h = s ∧ t.card = n

∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} {n : ℕ} [inst : DecidableEq α],
  s.card = n + 1 ↔ ∃ a t, a ∉ t ∧ insert a t = s ∧ t.card = n
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} [inst : DecidableEq α], s.card = 2 ↔ ∃ x y, x ≠ y ∧ s = {x, y}
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} [inst : DecidableEq α], s.card = 3 ↔ ∃ x y z, x ≠ y ∧ x ≠ z ∧ y ≠ z ∧ s = {x, y, z}

∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α} [inst : DecidableEq α],
  s.card = 4 ↔ ∃ x y z w, x ≠ y ∧ x ≠ z ∧ x ≠ w ∧ y ≠ z ∧ y ≠ w ∧ z ≠ w ∧ s = {x, y, z, w}
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, 2 < s.card ↔ ∃ a b c, a ∈ s ∧ b ∈ s ∧ c ∈ s ∧ a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ b ≠ c
∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α}, 2 < s.card ↔ ∃ a ∈ s, ∃ b ∈ s, ∃ c ∈ s, a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ b ≠ c

∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α},
  3 < s.card ↔ ∃ a b c d, a ∈ s ∧ b ∈ s ∧ c ∈ s ∧ d ∈ s ∧ a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ a ≠ d ∧ b ≠ c ∧ b ≠ d ∧ c ≠ d

∀ {α : Type u_1} {s : Finset α},
  3 < s.card ↔ ∃ a ∈ s, ∃ b ∈ s, ∃ c ∈ s, ∃ d ∈ s, a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ a ≠ d ∧ b ≠ c ∧ b ≠ d ∧ c ≠ d

doc:
Suppose that, given objects defined on all strict subsets of any finset `s`, one knows how to
define an object on `s`. Then one can inductively define an object on all finsets, starting from
the empty set and iterating. This can be used either to define data, or to prove properties.
statement:
{α : Type u_1} →
  {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} → ((s : Finset α) → ((t : Finset α) → t ⊂ s → p t) → p s) → (s : Finset α) → p s

∀ {α : Type u_1} {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} (H : (s : Finset α) → ((t : Finset α) → t ⊂ s → p t) → p s) (s : Finset α),
  Finset.strongInduction H s = H s fun t x => Finset.strongInduction H t

doc: Analogue of `strongInduction` with order of arguments swapped.
statement:
{α : Type u_1} →
  {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} → (s : Finset α) → ((s : Finset α) → ((t : Finset α) → t ⊂ s → p t) → p s) → p s

∀ {α : Type u_1} {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} (s : Finset α) (H : (s : Finset α) → ((t : Finset α) → t ⊂ s → p t) → p s),
  s.strongInductionOn H = H s fun t x => t.strongInductionOn H

∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq α] {p : Finset α → Prop} (s : Finset α),
  p ∅ → (∀ (a : α) (s : Finset α), a ∉ s → (∀ t ⊆ s, p t) → p (insert a s)) → p s

doc:
Suppose that, given objects defined on all nonempty strict subsets of any nontrivial finset `s`,
one knows how to define an object on `s`. Then one can inductively define an object on all finsets,
starting from singletons and iterating.

TODO: Currently this can only be used to prove properties.
Replace `Finset.Nonempty.exists_eq_singleton_or_nontrivial` with computational content
in order to let `p` be `Sort`-valued.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} {p : (s : Finset α) → s.Nonempty → Prop},
  (∀ (a : α), p {a} ⋯) →
    (∀ ⦃s : Finset α⦄ (hs : s.Nontrivial), (∀ (t : Finset α) (ht : t.Nonempty), t ⊂ s → p t ht) → p s ⋯) →
      ∀ ⦃s : Finset α⦄ (hs : s.Nonempty), p s hs

doc:
Suppose that, given that `p t` can be defined on all supersets of `s` of cardinality less than
`n`, one knows how to define `p s`. Then one can inductively define `p s` for all finsets `s` of
cardinality less than `n`, starting from finsets of card `n` and iterating. This
can be used either to define data, or to prove properties.
statement:
{α : Type u_1} →
  {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} →
    {n : ℕ} →
      ((t₁ : Finset α) → ({t₂ : Finset α} → t₂.card ≤ n → t₁ ⊂ t₂ → p t₂) → t₁.card ≤ n → p t₁) →
        (s : Finset α) → s.card ≤ n → p s

doc: Analogue of `strongDownwardInduction` with order of arguments swapped.
statement:
{α : Type u_1} →
  {n : ℕ} →
    {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} →
      (s : Finset α) →
        ((t₁ : Finset α) → ({t₂ : Finset α} → t₂.card ≤ n → t₁ ⊂ t₂ → p t₂) → t₁.card ≤ n → p t₁) → s.card ≤ n → p s

∀ {α : Type u_1} {n : ℕ} {p : Finset α → Sort u_3} (s : Finset α)
  (H : (t₁ : Finset α) → ({t₂ : Finset α} → t₂.card ≤ n → t₁ ⊂ t₂ → p t₂) → t₁.card ≤ n → p t₁),
  (fun a => s.strongDownwardInductionOn H a) = H s fun {t} ht x => t.strongDownwardInductionOn H ht
∀ {α : Type u_3}, WellFounded LT.lt

doc:
To prove a proposition for an arbitrary `Finset α`,
it suffices to prove that for any `S : Finset α`, the following is true:
the property is true for S with any element `s` removed, then the property holds for `S`.

This is a weaker version of `Finset.strongInduction`.
But it can be more precise when the induction argument
only requires removing single elements at a time.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq α] {p : Finset α → Prop},
  (∀ (S : Finset α), (∀ s ∈ S, p (S.erase s)) → p S) → ∀ (S : Finset α), p S

doc:
Given a function `f` which sends the finite set `s` to itself, the sequence of images of `s` under
iterates of `f` is eventually constant. Furthermore, the sequence of images stabilises in fewer
than `#s` steps.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq α] {f : α → α} {s : Finset α},
  Set.MapsTo f ↑s ↑s → s.Nonempty → ∃ n < s.card, ∀ (m : ℕ), n ≤ m → Finset.image f^[m] s = Finset.image f^[n] s

doc:
Given a function `f` which sends the finite set `s` to itself, the sequence of images of `s` under
iterates of `f` is eventually constant. Furthermore, the sequence of images stabilises in at most
`#s` steps.
statement:
∀ {α : Type u_1} [inst : DecidableEq α] {f : α → α} {s : Finset α},
  Set.MapsTo f ↑s ↑s → ∃ n ≤ s.card, ∀ (m : ℕ), n ≤ m → Finset.image f^[m] s = Finset.image f^[n] s
